     F. Systems and Methods for Managing DNSSEC 
     In some aspects, the present disclosure is directed to systems and methods for managing, enabling, or providing Domain Name Service Security (DNSSEC) to a zone in a Domain Name System (DNS). A DNS is a hierarchical naming system, for example, incorporating a distributed database for computers, services, resources and/or other entities connected by a network. The DNS may associate various information with domain names assigned to each of these entities. For example and in some embodiments, a DNS translates domain names that are meaningful to humans into numerical identifiers which may be associated with network devices. This translation may serve the purpose of locating and addressing these devices. 
     In some embodiments, DNS is implemented by the use of a set of resource records. Resource records may be any type or form of records. Each resource record (hereafter sometimes generally referred to as “RR” or “record”) may include any type or form of data, such as device, user and/or address data. For example, a resource record may include internet domain names, addresses and/or how these are related. In some embodiments, a resource record is a database record. By way of example, a set of resource records may include an address record (A), an IPv6 address record (AAAA), an AFS database record (AFSDB), an Address Prefix List (AFSDB), an Address Prefix List (APL), a Canonical name record (CNAME), a name server record (NS), a DNSSEC Lookaside Validation record (DLV), a DNS Key record (DNSKEY), a DNSSEC signature (RRSIG), a start of authority record (SOA), or any other type and form of record. 
     In some embodiments, a SOA record includes, provides and/or specifies authoritative information about a DNS zone. The information may include any combination of a primary name server, the email of the domain administrator, the domain serial number, one or more timers relating to refreshing the zone, etc. In certain embodiments, a NS record may include, provide, specify and/or delegate a DNS zone to use one or more given authoritative name servers. In some embodiments, a DLV record may include, provide, specify and/or publish DNSSEC trust anchors outside of a DNS delegation chain. A DLV record may use or have the same format as a DS record. RFC 5074 describes one or more ways of using these records. A or AAAA records may include, provide, specify and/or return an address that can be used for mapping hostnames to an IP address of a host. A RRSIG record includes, provides and/or specifies a signature for a DNSSEC-secured record set. 
     A number of records may be stored in one or more zone files of a DNS. A zone file may contain or describe mappings between domain names and IP addresses or other resources. These mappings may be organized in the form of text representations of resource records. In various embodiments, a DNS zone file is a file (e.g., text file) that describes a DNS zone. A DNS zone may be any subset of a hierarchical domain name structure of a DNS. In some embodiments, a DNS zone is a single domain. In some embodiments, a DNS zone is a portion of a DNS namespace for which administrative responsibility has been delegated. 
     A DNS namespace may be represented by a hierarchical tree like distribution of names with “.” (root) at the apex. A DNS namespace may be divided in hierarchical tree-like fashion into cascading lower-level domains. The lower-level domains may be ordered as a reverse-prioritized concatenation of names. Each level may be separated by a full stop and descending in priority written from right to left, e.g., a.b.c.com. A node's fully-qualified name may be obtained by traversing the tree up towards the root node and appending each encountered node's name with a “.” in between. Administratively, each level or node in the hierarchy may represent a potential boundary of authority for management of the name space. The authority over every level in every branch of the name space tree may be delegated to a legal entity or organization, such as a top-level country's domain registry, or a company or individual registered to use a given sub-domain in the system. These administrative spaces or portions of the domain name system are the DNS zones. Various aspects of the DNS namespace can be found in, for example, RFC 1034, “Domain Names—Concepts and Facilities”, and RFC 1035, “Domain Names—Implementation and Specification”. 
     Domain Name System Security or Domain Name System Security Extensions, hereafter sometimes generally referred to as “DNSSEC”), includes specifications for securing some types of information provided by a DNS for use in one or more networks. In some embodiments, DNSSEC is a set of extensions to DNS which provide source or origin authentication to DNS clients or resolvers. DNSSEC may also provide authenticated denial of existence. These features may be used to protect DNS clients from forged DNS data, for example. In certain embodiments, DNSSEC may provide data integrity, for example, by adding security features to DNS. DNSSEC may digitally sign some or all messages or answers for security reasons. A DNS client can check a corresponding digital signature to verify if information from a message is correct, complete and/or unaltered. In some embodiments, DNSSEC introduces or uses several record types to achieve its various objectives. These record types may include one or more of the following: 
     DNSKEY: This record can be a public component of a Zone Signing Key (ZSK) and/or Key Signing Key (KSK). These keys may be generated to sign a zone from DNSKEY records for the zone. These keys may be present at a zone apex. A zone apex may a top-level name in a zone, which is the name of the zone itself. For example, in foo.bar zone, foo.bar is the zone apex. All other names in foo.bar, such as host.foo.bar, are a level below foo.bar. In some embodiments, DNSKEY records are not found in some or all other records in the zone. The DNSKEY record may be included in a zone when the zone is signed. The ZSK and/or KSK keys may be added as part of an add key command associated with an intermediary appliance. 
     RRSIG: This record may be referred to as a signature record. When a zone is signed, each RRSet in the zone excluding glue records may be signed using the private component of a ZSK and the resulting signature kept in the RRSIG record. A RRSet may identify and/or include a set of records that have the same name, class and type for an RRSet. For example, foo.bar IN A 1.2.3.4; foo.bar IN A 1.2.3.5; foo.bar IN A 1.2.3.6. Since all these records have the same name, class (IN) and type (A), they may form an RRSet. An RRSIG record may be included in a zone when the zone is signed. RRSIG records can be generated as part of the signing process for a zone. 
     DS (Delegation Signer): This record can be a digest of the public component of the KSK. The system supports may support one or more digest algorithms: SHA-1 and SHA-256. In a system that supports two digest algorithms, it can result in two DS records per zone per key algorithm. These DS records may be installed along with NS records in the parent zone of the zone being signed. A DS record may be available when a zone is signed, although the record may not be included in the zone. This is because DS records may belong in the parent zone and are authoritative in the parent zone. Generated DS records may be provided to the parent zone through various means (email, phone, etc). These records may be added through a command-line interface (CLI) or GUI. 
     NSEC: This record may identify or define the next secure record in a zone. Records belonging to a zone to be signed may be arranged in canonical order by their names. An NSEC record may be added, for each name to point to the next name in the zone. If a query is received for the name b.foo.bar when the zone has a.foo.bar and d.foo.bar, then the response may indicate that no such name matches the query. The response may also include a NSEC record for d.foo.bar, the next record in the zone. The NSEC record may include a list of some or all types of RRs present that matches the name in query. This list may be empty for the above example querying for b.foo.bar. An empty list may further confirm that the queried name is a non-existent name. 
     NSEC3: This record may include features that may be similar to NSEC records. In some embodiments, instead of providing d.foo.bar in the above example, the NSEC3 record may provide a hashed representation of d.foo.bar. This record can be introduced to avoid or reduce the possibility of malicious clients using NSEC for zone enumeration when zone transfer is disabled. 
     DNSSEC may digitally sign one or more resource records for DNS lookup using public-key cryptography. A DNSKEY record is authenticated via a chain of trust, starting with a set of verified public keys for the DNS root zone which is the trusted third party. In some DNSSEC implementations, each answer to a DNS lookup may contain an RRSIG DNS record in addition to a record type that was requested. The RRSIG record may be a digital signature of the answer DNS resource record set. The digital signature may be verified by locating a correct public key found in a DNSKEY record. The DS record may be used in the authentication of DNSKEYs in a lookup procedure using the chain of trust. NSEC and NSEC3 records may be used for robust resistance against spoofing. The public key cryptographic approach referenced above may be characterized by the use of asymmetric key algorithms. A private key can be used to encrypt a message and is different from a public key that can be used to decrypt the message. The private key may be kept secret but the public key is distributed.

The DNSSEC manager may provide, enable and/or manage DNS security for various modes of a DNS zone or modes of operation for the DNS zone. The DNSSEC manager may include any hardware or combination of hardware and software. The DNSSEC manager may include an application, program, library, script, process, task, thread or any type and form of instructions for executing on hardware, e.g., a processor of the device  200 .      In some embodiments, the implement of DNS on intermediary device may allow DNS RRs to be added with it without creating or identifying zones. In the case where zones are not created, it is implied that a domain (e.g., foo.bar) in the DNS namespace has been delegated to the intermediary device if the domain is contained in a query received by the intermediary device. For example and in one embodiment, for a zone foo.bar, the device may have an entry in the “bar” zone indicating that the zone foo.bar is available at the device. Even though there is no zone identification or entity, the device may implement zone authority behavior when both SOA and NS records are configured for the zone foo.bar.

In the context of DNSSEC, a zone name may be useful information for providing certain DNSSEC features. A zone name may be part of signature records, for example. It may also be useful to have a zone name or zone entity to provide DNS Zone transfer support. The intermediary device can use a zone entity of a zone to identify configured records belonging to the zone. By way of illustration, and in one embodiment, if foo.bar is a configured zone, then RRs that end with foo.bar (e.g., host1.foo.bar, host1.foochild1.foo.bar) may belong to this zone. In another embodiment, where a sub-zone is delegated out to other DNS servers, there could be a zone, foochild2.foo.bar, that is delegated to other DNS servers.      The DNSSEC manager may manage any type or form of DNS messages, including but not limited to receipt and processing of queries, and generation and transmission of responses. When the DNSSEC manager receives a query for a configured name (e.g., zone name), a response with an answer may be sent. When a query is for a name (e.g., zone name) that does not exist, an error, such as a “no such name” error, may be sent. 
     The DNSSEC manager of the device may provide one or more modes for an identified zone. Such modes may be referred to variously as modes of operation, DNS modes, zone modes, or similar nomenclature. The one or more modes may include an authoritative mode and a proxy mode, discussed in more detail below. The one or more modes may be part of a zone configuration of the system or device. The DNSSEC manager may enable DNSSEC support for a zone via a zone configuration of the zone. When DNSSEC support is enabled, the DNSSEC manager can decide if a signed record may be sent to a client requesting signed records. 
     The DNSSEC manager may provide an authoritative mode for an identified zone. In some embodiments, the authoritative mode comprises a type, classification or group of one or more modes. For example, the authoritative mode may include or support an ADNS mode, DNS Proxy mode, a recursive resolver mode and/or a stub resolver mode. In the authoritative mode, the SOA and/or NS records for the zone may be configured on the intermediary device or a DNS server of the device. Other records belonging to the zone may also be configured. In some embodiments, a zone may be configured in the authoritative mode in both ADNS and DNS Proxy deployment modes. 
     In some embodiments, the DNSSEC manager supports an ADNS mode. In the ADNS mode, the intermediary device may be configured to be the authority for a zone. An authoritative name server, or name server operating in authoritative mode or providing an authoritative zone, may provide answers to DNS queries for domain names within its zone of authority, the answers configured by an original source such as an administrator or via dynamic DNS methods, as opposed to answers obtained from DNS queries from the name server to another name server. The intermediary device may include or have some or all records for the zone. One illustrative and non-limiting embodiment of steps involved in this mode may include: (i) adding a mandatory zone record (e.g., with options proxyMode NO and DNSSEC ENABLED; (ii) add mandatory SOA and NS records for the zone; (iii) adding some or all the records that belong to the zone; (iv) creating keys for signing records; (v) signing the zone; and/or getting DS records for the zone for installing in the parent zone. Under this and/or other modes, the zone may be available to respond to DNSSEC queries. 
     In some embodiments, the DNSSEC manager supports a DNS Proxy mode. In the DNS Proxy mode, the intermediary device may load balance a plurality of backend DNS servers. Some or all zone information and authority may reside with the DNS servers. The intermediary device may forward new queries to the backend servers and cache their responses to be served out subsequently from the cache, e.g., to a client. There may be several ways to use or apply this mode. In contrast to an authoritative name server or master or slave DNS servers, a proxy mode name server receives client queries and forwards the request to another name server. Upon receipt of an answer from the name server, the proxy caches the answer and forwards the result back to the client. Although referred to as a client, one of skill in the art may readily envision similar forwarding and proxying of requests via servers, clients, or other intermediaries. Proxying of DNS requests allows local caching by the proxy to speed up response times, as well as providing load balancing for a plurality of name servers. For example, by placing a single proxy in front of several name servers and forwarding incoming requests to the name servers in a round-robin fashion, a greater number of simultaneous clients may be served via a single name server address provided by the proxy. 
     In certain embodiments, some zone records are configured on the intermediary device. Some or most records, such as the SOA and/or NS records, may reside on the backend servers. Some records may be configured on the intermediary device. This configuration or setup may be used in a GSLB context. For example, some or all records may be present in a backend server except for domains that GSLB is performed. One illustrative and non-limiting embodiment of steps involved in this mode or configuration are as follows: 
     On the intermediary device, (i) mandatory zone records may be added (e.g., with options proxyMode YES and DNSSEC ENABLED); (ii) SOA and/or NS records may not be added in some embodiments; (iii) records that belong to the zone may be added, to be served out by the intermediary device; (iv) Keys from a backend server may be imported; (v) the zone may be signed; and (v) in some embodiments, the intermediary may not generate DS records. On the backend DNS Server(s), such as in a proxy mode of operation, operations may include (i) adding the zone and some or all the records; (ii) including records configured on the intermediary device in the zone; (iii) creating keys; (iv) signing the zone; (v) exporting keys to the intermediary device; and/or getting the DS records for the zone for installing in the parent zone. 
     In certain embodiments, no records may be configured on the intermediary device. In this mode, no configuration may be performed on the DNSSEC manager and/or intermediary device. The intermediary device may, for example, simply cache DNSSEC records received from backend servers and serve them out in subsequent queries for them. 
     The DNSSEC manager may provide a proxy mode for an identified zone. In some embodiments, the proxy mode comprises a type, classification or group of one or more modes. For example, the proxy mode may include or support one or more modes described above, such as the ADNS mode, DNS Proxy mode, recursive resolver mode and/or a stub resolver mode. In the proxy mode, the SOA and/or NS records may be configured on one or more backend servers, or servers to which the device serves as an intermediary with at least one client. A zone may be configured in the proxy mode, for example when a DNS Proxy deployment mode is used. 
     In some embodiments, a mode flag of the zone provides validation during signing (e.g., of a message), such as to make sure that the corresponding SOA and/or NS records are configured. Accordingly, and as discussed above, different signing methods may be used for different zones simultaneously. For example, the intermediary may act in a proxy mode for a first zone, and forward requests to name servers which may sign answers. The proxy may forward the answers to requesting clients directly. The intermediary may also act in authoritative mode for a second zone and directly resolve and sign DNS answers. Accordingly, the intermediary may provide DNSSEC to both zones under its authority and zones for which it acts as a proxy. 
     The system may provide enhanced or modified DNS features for supporting DNSSEC. In some embodiments, one such feature may be referred to as an Extension mechanism for DNS or EDNS0. EDNS0 support may allow a client to indicate a (e.g., larger) maximum UDP payload that a DNS response can contain for the client to re-assemble and process. For example, the original DNS specification may limit the payload of a response or message to 512 bytes. With EDNS0, clients may accept payloads up to 4096 bytes, for example, although any size may be configured. Without EDNS0, the larger responses required for communication of keys in DNSSEC may not fit in a single UDP payload, and may instead need to be provided over one or more TCP payloads to be reassembled by the recipient, adding overhead and decreasing efficiency. 
     In some embodiments, the DNSSEC manager sends a FORMAT ERROR indicator when a query is received with EDNS0's OPT records in another section. This behavior may be found, for example, in servers that do not support EDNS0 or have EDNS0 enabled. In certain embodiments, EDNS0 support may be desired to support DNSSEC. In some embodiments, DNSSEC may cause response sizes to increase. Restriction to the response size, such as restriction to 512 bytes, may cause some clients to retry one or more times in TCP mode in order to get a complete answer. In some embodiments, the DNSSEC manager is configured to support sending and receiving UDP payload sizes of 4096 bytes or larger. 
     In some embodiments, EDNS0 support may be available by default. If a client indicates that it supports or conforms to EDNS0, the intermediary device may send a UDP response that is the smaller of the client's EDNS0 payload support size and 4096 bytes. If the response exceeds this size, a TC flag may be set in the response. In response to the TC Flag, the client may be expected to send the query again in TCP. 
     If the response is not in intermediary device's cache, the intermediary device may forward the corresponding request to the backend server(s) in proxy mode. The intermediary device may verify and/or ensure that the EDNS0 payload support size is the minimum of the client EDNS0 payload support size and 4096 bytes. In some embodiments, the intermediary device may forward the client query without any change to the payload size. In certain embodiments, EDNS0 settings of the server and/or intermediary device are not stored or tracked, e.g., by each other. EDNS0 settings may be queried based upon need. 
     In some embodiments, the DNSSEC manager includes or communicates with a key generator. The DNSSEC manager may use public key cryptographic techniques for signing records in a zone. The DNSSEC manager and/or key generator may provide commands, instructions and/or configurations for generating keys for a zone. In some embodiments, a moderate-size (e.g., 1024 bytes) Zone signing Key (ZSK) may be used to sign the RRs in a zone. In certain embodiments, a strong size (e.g., 4096 bytes) Key Signing Key (KSK) may be used to sign the ZSK and/or KSK. As referred to herein, strong and moderate size keys may reflect relative differences rather than specific sizes. The KSK may make a digest of itself and/or the ZSK. The digest may be available to the parent for clients or resolvers to create authentication chains. In some embodiments, a same key may be used for the ZSK and KSK.

         a. 2048 bit RSA,   b. Rolled over 2-5 years.   c. SHA-256 based signatures

     In brief overview of one embodiment of public key cryptography, each key may include a pair of components. A key may include a private component and a public component. The intermediary device may provide a mechanism to generate keys for a zone. The keys that are generated may be stored in a cache or storage (e.g., flash memory) of the intermediary device (e.g., for a CITRIX NETSCALER product, at /nsconfig/dns/<zoneName>). The key generator may generate two files per key, for example, one for the private component and another for the public component. 
     The key generator may include, support, use or apply one or more key algorithms, such as RSASHA1, RSASHA256 and RSASHA512. Multiple key algorithms can be used under particular modes, configuration and/or with particular clients. In some embodiments, a number of key files (e.g., zsk-private, zsk-public, ksk-private, and ksk-public) per key algorithm may be generated and stored by the intermediary device. 
     The DNSSEC manager may sign a zone, e.g., via a signer or an administrative entity. Signing a zone may involve one or more steps. One illustrative and non-limiting embodiment of steps includes: (i) identifying the zone to sign and RRSets that belong to the zone; (ii) arranging the RRSet owner names (e.g., in canonical order); adding public key components (e.g., as DNSKEY RR) to the zone; (iii) adding NSEC RR for each name (e.g., to indicate the canonically next secure name); (iv) using a private key to generate a signature for each RRSet in the zone and adding it as an RRSIG RR; (v) generating the DS RR's and storing them (e.g., in a file in /nsconfig/dns/<ZoneName>directory). 
     The DNSSEC manager may use one or more RRs for security in communications between a DNS Client and a DNS Server. One or more other RRs may be defined for security in communications between DNS Servers. By way of illustration, communications between DNS Servers may include Dynamic updates, Zone transfers, etc. A DNS Server may communicate with another DNS Server via or bypassing the intermediary device, for example in DNS Proxy Mode. Records that are used for Server-Server security may include TSIG, SIG(0), TKEY, etc. The intermediary device may pass these RRs through in Proxy mode. Some of these RRs may have limited support, or no support in certain modes, for example, in ADNS mode and/or recursive resolver mode. 
     In some embodiments, the DNSSEC manager may provide DNSSEC Look-aside Validation (DLV) support. DLV feature may be used in certain mode, e.g., resolver modes. To support DNSSEC in a zone, DS records may be installed in the parent zone. In some embodiments, if the parent zone does not support DNSSEC, the parent zone may not be able to provide DS records. In some of these embodiments, a signed zone may be managed as if it is unsigned. Signed zones with unsigned parent zones are sometimes referred to as Islands of Security. DLV support may enable signed domains with unsigned parents to register with Internet Systems Consortium (ISC) to create equivalents for DS records. 
     In some embodiments, the intermediary device may return DNSSEC records in a response to a client's query. The client may indicate in the query that it can accept DNSSEC records. This may be done, for example, by setting the DO (DNSSEC OK) bit flag in the OPT RR. The signer or administrator may sign the zone. The administrator or signer may enable the DNSSEC flag on the zone configuration. 
     Zone maintenance is a part of administering signed zones on a DNS Server. The intermediary device may include one or more of the following aspects with regards to zone maintenance: High Availability (HA) behavior, re-signing RR's on addition or modification, Zone SOA update, and Key rollover. HA behavior may refer to the system's ability to handle high or increased levels of DNS operations, such as processing a plurality of queries and sending responses to the queries. HA behavior may include load balancing, configuring a backup intermediary, or performing other functions to provide service availability in case of failure of a primary intermediary. Accordingly, in some embodiments, the system may include a plurality of intermediate devices. For example and in one embodiment, a new node may be added as a HA partner to an existing unit that is working standalone. One of the plurality of intermediate devices may be designated as a primary (e.g., for DNS operations). Another of the plurality of intermediate devices may be designated as a secondary. DNS and other operations may be distributed across at least a primary and a secondary, for example by a global server load balancing (GSLB) process or device. In some embodiments, a secondary may also act as a failover for a primary. Apart from GSLB, the intermediary device may interoperate with other modules, e.g., providing IPv6, SNMP and/or other features. 
     In some embodiments, the system supports a propagation mode with respect to DNSKEY records. Cryptographic keys may be generated on a primary and synchronized to a secondary. The public keys may be added into a zone as DNSKEY records. For example, the public keys may be added into the zone by or responsive to a “add dns keys” command executed on both the primary and secondary. The key files may be created as part of the “create keys” command and may be synchronized before an add command is executed. In some embodiments, the create command may not be propagated to the secondary. After creating the key files, the key files may be resynchronized to the secondary. The DNSSEC manager of the primary may wait until the resynchronization is complete to return the command. A sequence of checks may be performed during the command to add the keys into the zone. The directory where the keys are stored in memory or storage may be identified by the file synchronization process. 
     In some embodiments, the system supports a synchronization mode with respect to DNSKEY records. Between a primary and a secondary intermediary, file synchronization and configuration synchronization can happen simultaneously, sequentially or independently. In one embodiment, an Add command may be executed before file synchronization happens when no key files exist. When the add command is executed and no file is specified in the directory, the add command may fail on the secondary. The secondary may continue its configuration synchronization. Because of a failed command, a mismatch of HA configuration version numbers may happen in some embodiments. This may cause the secondary to clear its configuration and re-initiate configuration-synchronization. 
     In another embodiment, an Add command may be executed before the file synchronization happens and an old file may exists. The DNSSEC manager may attempt to identify that the file in keys directory is same as that in the primary. The primary may include a key-id in the add dns key command issued to the secondary. This may cause the add dns key to fail. This failure may cause re-synchronization of the configuration. 
     In still another embodiment, an Add command may be executed before file synchronization happens but a partial new file may exist. DNSSEC manager may attempt to verify if the key file is or is not a partial file. For example, a key file can be checked for completeness or validity. In some embodiments, md5 may be synchronized from the primary and checked on the secondary. If the md5 does not exist or does not match the generated md5 for the file, the key file may be identified as partial. The Add command may fail as a consequence. This failure may cause re-synchronization of the configuration. In some embodiments, the DNSSEC manager may open a keyfile in write mode, so that partial writes (e.g., by another operation) may be prevented. If a file synchronization is already writing, add dns key may not be able to open the file and can fail. If add dns key is reading the key file, file synchronization may fail. 
     In yet another embodiment, an Add command may be executed after file synchronization. In certain embodiments, this may be a better mode than others. The public file contents may be added as DNSKEYS on the secondary. 
     Accordingly, through the above embodiments, configuration and DNSSEC keys may be transferred from a primary intermediary to one or more secondary, backup, or alternate intermediaries, allowing high availability behavior in case of failure of the primary, as well as load balancing and other features. 
     In some embodiments, the system supports a propagation mode with respect to DS records. When the sign command is executed, DS records may be created, e.g., by the DNSSEC manager. The DNSSEC manager may create two DS records per KSK. A digest may be generated with SHA1. Another digest may be generated with SHA256, for example. Apart from generating DS records for the zone that the DNSSEC manager signs, the DNSSEC manager can also have DS records for secure zones that it delegates. In this case DS records may be provided by a corresponding child zone. 
     DS records may be created and/or added. With created DS records, the intermediary device (e.g., primary) may generate RRSIG and NSEC records as part of signing. The intermediary device may instruct the DNSSEC manager to generate DS records for the KSKs. After the DS keys are generated, the DS keys may be rsync-ed to the secondary. The key files may be present in the directory that is synced by a file sync process. With added DS records, if the intermediary device is delegating a secure domain, the intermediary device may add DS records for the child zone through configuration. When DS records are added through the configuration, the Add command may be propagated to the secondary and added to the secondary. 
     In some embodiments, the system supports a synchronization mode with respect to DS records. With created DS records, a file sync process may synchronize these DS records to the secondary. With added DS records, a configuration synchronization may synchronize the DS records to the secondary. 
     In some embodiments, the system supports a propagation mode with respect to RRSIG and/or NSEC records. In other embodiments, the system may not support a propagation mode with respect to RRSIG and/or NSEC records. For example, RRSIG and/or NSEC records may not be propagated to the secondary. When the sign command is propagated, the secondary independently generates the RRSIG and/or NSEC records. 
     In some embodiments, the system supports a synchronization mode with respect to RRSIG and/or NSEC records. In other embodiments, the system may not support a synchronization mode with respect to RRSIG and/or NSEC records. For example, RRSIG and/or NSEC records may not be synchronized to the secondary. When the sign command is synchronized to the secondary, the secondary may independently generate the RRSIG and/or NSEC records. 
     In some embodiments, a zone may have to be re-signed when changes are made to the signed zone. For example, the intermediary device may automatically sign a modified or newly added record. After modifications are made to the zone, the “sign dns zone” command may be explicitly called to sign the modified or new record. 
     When a zone record is changed or updated, a serial number in the SOA record may have to be changed. When changes are made in a signed zone, the serial number can be automatically updated, for example, by incrementing the serial by 1 each time, or by setting the current time as the serial number. The DNSSEC manager may store the serial number across reboots, if the serial number is updated automatically or otherwise. In some embodiments, the serial number update is done manually after RR changes. 
     In some embodiments, where the system includes a standalone intermediary device providing DNSSEC features, one or more of the following may occur. In one embodiment, a change or addition of a record to a zone may set the SOA serial to the current time. A ‘Sign dns zone” command may cause the SOA serial number to be set to the current time. A “Saveconfig’ command may save the serial number in a SOA record. Auto-rollover and/or re-signing may cause the serial number to be set to current time. In one embodiments, a Saveconfig command may not be called, so the new serial number may not be stored (e.g., in ns.conf but kept in memory). On a reboot, the intermediary device may read the configuration on boot-up. As commands are added, a SOA record may be set to the current time. If zone transfer is supported, the secondary may initiate synchronization (e.g., regardless of whether changes occurred). 
     In some embodiments, the system includes a HA setup. DNS commands propagated and/or synchronized from the primary to secondary may have a serial number embedded. The secondary may use this number as a serial number in the secondary's SOA record for the zone. 
     In some embodiments, the system includes a remote GSLB site with an intermediary device running on it. As part of a zone synchronization, the DNSSEC manager of the device may synchronize the key files. The DNSSEC manager may synchronize the whole zone, and may include passing the SOA serial number. In some embodiments, a DNS Daemon may be setup for signing a corresponding zone. The DNSSEC manager may use both zone transfer and key transfer. 
     In some embodiments, RRSIG records may have an expiry period. When they expire, RRSets may have to be re-signed with a new key. A mechanism may be put in place to rollover the keys. The intermediary and/or the DNSSEC manager may provide one or more of the following: Manual Key rollover, Pre-Publish, Double-Sign, ZSK Rollover, KSK Rollover, Emergency Key Rollover, ZSK Rollover, etc. 
     In a ZSK Rollover, the DNSSEC manager may add a new ZSK to a zone. The DNSSEC manager may sign the zone with the new ZSK and existing KSK. If the KSK is in a rollover phase, the DNSSEC may honor the rollover and/or sign with a KSK (e.g., present in the /nsconfig/dns). 
     In a KSK Rollover, the DNSSEC manager may keep the Chain of Trust. The DNSSEC manager may add anew KSK but continue to keep a compromised KSK. The DNSSEC manager may sign the DNSKEY records with the new KSK (e.g., with short validity). The DNSSEC manager may upload the DS record of the new key to the parent. The DNSSEC manager may wait for the new DS to appear in slave name servers for the zone and TTL of old DS records. The DNSSEC manager may remove the compromised DNSKEY RR from the zone and re-sign with normal validity. The DNSSEC manager may apply a sign zone command with delay. 
     In a KSK Rollover, the DNSSEC manager may keep the Chain of Trust. The DNSSEC manager may break the Chain of Trust. The DNSSEC manager may make the child zone appear Bogus. The DNSSEC manager may replace the KSK and sign with the new KSK. The DNSSEC manager may send the new DS to the parent. Before the parent updates the DS, the child zone may appear Bogus. The DNSSEC manager may make the child zone appear insecure. The DNSSEC manager may remove the DS record from parent zone. Responsive to the removal, the child zone may appear insecure.

     RFC4033: DNS Security Introduction and Requirements 
     RFC4034: Resource Records for the DNS Security Extensions 
     RFC4035: Protocol Modifications for the DNS Security Extensions 
     RFC4641: DNSSEC Operational Practices

     Referring now to  FIG. 6B , a flow diagram depicts embodiments of steps taken in a method  600  for providing multiple modes of a zone for DNSSEC by an intermediary device. The method includes providing, by a device intermediary to a plurality of clients and a plurality of servers, a plurality of modes of a zone for Domain Name Service ( 601 ). The device receives a selection of a first mode of the zone of the plurality of modes of the zone ( 603 ). The device receives information identifying to enable DNS Security for the selected first mode ( 605 ). The device establishes the zone for DNS in accordance with the selected first mode and with DNS Security enabled ( 607 ). 
     In further details of ( 601 ), a device intermediary to a plurality of clients and a plurality of servers, provides a plurality of modes of a zone for DNS. The device may provide a plurality of modes, including an authoritative and/or a proxy mode. The device may provide a plurality of mode types or classifications, including authoritative and/or proxy. The device may provide and/or support any one or more of: an ADNS mode, a DNS Proxy mode, a recursive resolver mode, and a stub resolver mode. The device may be configured (e.g., via a command-line interface) by one or more configurations for each supported mode. The device may incorporate or support EDNS0 features. The device may create or add one or more resource records. An administrator or user may create or add one or more resource records to the device and/or zone. The device may be configured to be the authority for the zone. 
     In further details of ( 603 ), the device receives a selection of one mode of the zone from the plurality of modes of operation, management, or administration of the zone, sometimes referred to as a mode of the zone, such as proxy mode or authoritative mode. An administrator or user may identify one or more modes to enable in the DNSSEC manager of the device. An administrator or user may identify or select a mode via an interface (e.g., a command-line interface) of the device. An administrator or user may select or configure a mode to enable via one or more configuration files processed by the device. The device may add any records (e.g., mandatory records) for the zone. 
     At step ( 605 ), the device receives information identifying to enable DNS Security for the selected first mode. The device may receive commands and/or configurations from an administrator or user to support DNSSEC features. The device may receive or add a mandatory zone record specifying that DNSSEC be enabled. The device may receive updates to the device, for example DNSSEC-related resource records. The device may add any records (e.g., mandatory records), related to DNSSEC, for the zone. The device may receive configuration indicating to select one or more encryption methods. The device may receive configuration for the device to sign the zone. 
     In further details of ( 607 ), the device establishes the zone for DNS in accordance with the selected first mode and with DNS Security enabled. The device may configure the zone with DNS security enabled, responsive to receiving the information identifying to enable DNS Security. The device may perform any one or more steps described above in connection with the selected mode. The device may be configured (e.g., by an administrator or used) to be the authority for the zone. The device may configure the zone with DNS security enabled, responsive to configuration indicating to select one or more encryption methods. The device may configure the zone with DNS security enabled, responsive to receiving DNSSEC-related records (e.g., from a backend server). The device may configure the zone with DNS security enabled, responsive to receiving, importing or generating keys. The device may sign the zone using the keys to provide DNS with security. 
     It should be understood that the systems described above may provide multiple ones of any or each of those components and these components may be provided on either a standalone machine or, in some embodiments, on multiple machines in a distributed system. In addition, the systems and methods described above may be provided as one or more computer-readable programs or executable instructions embodied on or in one or more articles of manufacture. The article of manufacture may be a floppy disk, a hard disk, a CD-ROM, a flash memory card, a PROM, a RAM, a ROM, or a magnetic tape. In general, the computer-readable programs may be implemented in any programming language, such as LISP, PERL, C, C++, C#, PROLOG, or in any byte code language such as JAVA. The software programs or executable instructions may be stored on or in one or more articles of manufacture as object code. 
     While the invention has been particularly shown and described with reference to specific embodiments, it should be understood by those skilled in the art that various changes in form and detail may be made therein without departing from the spirit and scope of this disclosure.

cases.title: Methods and Systems for TDD PUCCH HARQ Resourse Allocation for Enhanced Physical Downlink Control Channel (EPDCCH)
cases.abstract: PUCCH resource determination for HARQ-ACK transmission in response to ePDCCH-scheduled PDSCH or ePDCCH-indicated SPS release in a TDD radio communication system. Downlink control information (DCI) is received in a downlink subframe via an Enhanced Physical Downlink Control Channel (ePDCCH). A resource index for a Physical Uplink Control Channel (PUCCH) resource is determined, based on the lowest enhanced Control Channel Element (eCCE) index of the received DCI, a device-specific offset value, and an index i that identifies the downlink subframe in a pre-determined set of one or more downlink subframes associated with an uplink subframe. The PUCCH resource is determined according to a formula that results in a sequential allocation of PUCCH resources in the uplink subframe with respect to the downlink subframes associated with the uplink subframe, for each of a plurality of sets of ePDCCH resources. HARQ feedback is transmitted in the uplink subframe, in the indexed PUCCH resource.

cases.description:
TECHNICAL FIELD 
     The present invention generally relates to wireless communication networks, and particularly relates to the allocation of uplink control channel resources within such networks. 
     BACKGROUND 
     The 3rd-Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) has developed specifications for a fourth-generation wireless communications technology known as “Long Term Evolution,” or “LTE.” LTE uses Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) in the downlink and DFT-spread OFDM in the uplink, where DFT denotes “Discrete Fourier Transform”. The basic LTE physical resources can thus be seen as a time-frequency grid, as illustrated in  FIG. 1 , where each resource element corresponds to one subcarrier during one OFDM symbol interval on a particular antenna port. An antenna port is defined such that the channel over which a symbol on the antenna port is conveyed can be inferred from the channel over which another symbol on the same antenna port is conveyed. There is one resource grid per antenna port. 
     In the time domain, LTE downlink transmissions are organized into radio frames of ten milliseconds. Each radio frame includes ten equally sized subframes of one millisecond.  FIG. 2  illustrates this arrangement one sees from the diagram that each subframe is divided into two slots, with each slot having a duration of 0.5 milliseconds. 
     Resource allocation in LTE is described in terms of “Physical Resource Blocks,” or “PRBs.” As shown in  FIG. 3 , a PRB corresponds to one slot in the time domain and twelve contiguous 15-kHz subcarriers in the frequency domain. The bandwidth, N BW , of the overall system determines the number of PRBs in each slot, and each PRB spans six or seven OFDM symbols, depending upon the length of the cyclic prefix (CP) used. Two consecutive PRBs in time represent a PRB pair. User scheduling by the LTE base station, referred to as an “eNodeB” or “eNB”, is generally performed using the PRB pair as the smallest unit of resource allocation. 
     Transmissions in LTE are dynamically scheduled based on transmitting downlink assignments and uplink grants to targeted mobile terminals (referred to as “user equipment,” or “UEs,” in 3GPP terminology). According to Release 8 of the 3GPP standards, which was the first release to include specifications for LTE, the downlink assignments and uplink grants are transmitted in a defined control region using Physical Downlink Control Channels (PDCCHs) targeted to specific UEs. The search space for PDCCH reception, which defines those resources in any given subframe that might include control information for the UEs, is known to the UEs. The UEs thus blindly decode those portions of the received signal to find PDCCHs targeted to them. 
     More broadly, PDCCHs are used to convey UE-specific scheduling assignments for the downlink and uplink grants, as noted, and are further used for Physical Random Access Channel (PRACH) responses, uplink power control commands, and common scheduling assignments for signaling messages that include, among other things, system information and paging. 
       FIG. 4  illustrates that a “normal” downlink subframe includes a control region at the beginning of the subframe, followed by a data region. The size of the control region in which PDCCHs are transmitted can vary in size from one to four OFDM symbols in dependence on the involved configuration. A Physical Control Format Indicator (PCFICH) is used to indicate the control region length and is transmitted within the control region at locations known by the UEs. A UE thus learns the size of the control region in a given downlink subframe by decoding the PCFICH transmitted in that subframe, and therefore knows in which OFDM symbol the data transmission starts. 
     PDCCHs are made up of Control Channel Elements (CCEs), where each CCE consists of nine Resource Element Groups (REGs). Each REG in turn consists of four resource elements (REs). LTE defines four PDCCH formats 0-3, which use aggregation levels of 1, 2, 4, and 8 CCEs, respectively. Given the modulation format used for PDCCH transmission, two bits can be transmitted on each individual RE aggregated within a PDCCH; with 1 CCE=9 REGs=36 REs and 2 bits/symbol, one can transmit 72 bits via a format 0 PDCCH, 144 bits via a format 1 PDCCH, etc. As noted, PDCCHs are transmitted in the defined control region—the first 1-4 symbols—of any given downlink subframe and extend over substantially the entire system bandwidth. Thus, the size of the control region in the given downlink subframe and the overall system bandwidth define the number of overall CCEs available for PDCCH transmission. 
       FIG. 4  also illustrates the presence of Cell-specific Reference Symbols (CRS) within the downlink subframe. The locations and values of CRS are known by the UEs, which use the received CRS for estimation of the radio channel. The channel estimates are in turn used in the demodulation of data by the UEs. CRS are also used for mobility measurements performed by the UEs. 
     Because the CRS are common to all UEs in a cell, the transmission of CRS cannot be easily adapted to suit the needs of a particular UE. Therefore, LTE also supports UE-specific reference symbols generally intended only for assisting channel estimation for demodulation purposes. These UE-specific RS are referred to as Demodulation Reference Symbols (DMRS). DMRS for a particular UE are placed in the data region of the downlink subframe, as part of Physical Downlink Shared Channel (PDSCH) transmissions. 
     Release 11 of the 3GPP standards introduced the enhanced PDCCH (ePDCCH) as an additional, and more flexible, channel for transmitting control messages to UEs. An ePDCCH uses resources in the data region associated with PDSCH transmissions, rather than resource elements within the defined control region at the beginning of the subframe. See “Universal Mobile Telecommunications System (UMTS); Technical Specifications and Technical Reports for a UTRAN-based 3GPP system”, 3GPP TS 21.101, v.11.0.0. 
       FIG. 5  provides a basic illustration of PRB pairs allocated from the data region of a downlink subframe, for use in the transmission of given ePDCCHs. The remaining PRB pairs in the data portion of the subframe can be used for PDSCH transmissions; hence the ePDCCH transmissions are frequency multiplexed with PDSCH transmissions. That arrangement differs from PDCCH transmissions, which are time multiplexed with respect to PDSCH transmissions—i.e., PDCCH transmissions occur only in the control portion of the downlink subframe, which occurs in time before the data portion in which PDSCH transmissions are performed. 
     Resource allocation for PDSCH transmissions can be according to several resource allocation types, depending on the downlink control information (DCI) format. Some resource allocation types have a minimum scheduling granularity of a resource block group (RBG). An RBG is a set of adjacent (in frequency) resource blocks. When scheduling the UE according to these resource allocation types, the UE is allocated resources in terms of RBGs, rather than according to individual resource blocks (RBs) or RB pairs. 
     When a UE is scheduled in the downlink from an ePDCCH, the UE shall assume that the PRB pairs carrying the downlink assignment are excluded from the resource allocation, i.e., rate matching applies. For example, if a UE is scheduled to receive PDSCH in a certain RBG that consists of three adjacent PRB pairs, and if one of these PRB pairs contains the downlink assignment, then the UE shall assume that the PDSCH is transmitted in only the two remaining PRB pairs in this RBG. Notably, Release 11 does not support multiplexing of PDSCH and ePDCCH transmission within the same PRB pair. 
     ePDCCH messages are made up of enhanced Control Channel Elements (eCCEs), which are analogous to the CCEs used in the PDCCH. For purposes of mapping ePDCCH messages to PRB pairs, each PRB pair is divided into sixteen enhanced resource element groups (eREGs). Each eCCE is made up of four or eight of these eREGs, for normal and extended cyclic prefix, respectively. An ePDCCH is consequently mapped to a multiple of either four or eight eREGs, depending on the aggregation level. The eREGs belonging to a particular ePDCCH resides in either a single PRB pair (as is typical for localized transmission) or a multiple of PRB pairs (as is typical for distributed transmission). 
     One example of the possible division of a PRB pair into eREGs is illustrated in  FIG. 6 , which illustrates an unconstrained subframe. Each block or tile in the figure is an individual resource element (RE) and the tile number corresponds to the EREG that the RE is grouped within. For example, tiles having the dotted background all belong to same EREG indexed at  0 . 
     A UE can be configured so that multiple sets of PRB pairs are available for use as ePDCCH resources. Each ePDCCH resource set consists of N=2, 4, or 8 PRB pairs. In addition, two modes of ePDCCH transmission are supported, i.e., localized and distributed ePDCCH transmission. Each set of ePDCCH resources is independently configured as being of localized or distributed type. In distributed transmission, an ePDCCH is mapped to resource elements in an ePDCCH set in a distributed manner, i.e., using multiple PRB pairs that are separated from each other in frequency. In this way, frequency diversity can be achieved for the ePDCCH message. As of Release 11, the ePDCCH can be mapped to resource elements in up to D PRB pairs, where D=2, 4, or 8 (the value of D=16 is also being considered in 3GPP).  FIG. 7A  illustrates an example of distributed transmission, where D=4 is illustrated. As seen in the example, the ePDCCH is divided into four parts, which are mapped to different PRB pairs. These four parts may correspond to eCCEs, for example. 
     In a localized transmission, on the other hand, an ePDCCH is mapped to one PRB pair only, if the space allows. Mapping to a single PRB pair is always possible for aggregation levels one and two, and is possible also for aggregation level four for the case of a normal, “unconstrained” subframe and a normal CP length. Here, an “unconstrained” or normal subframe is one having a PDSCH region that is not abbreviated. Constrained subframes include “special” subframes in TDD LTE that include uplink and downlink portions, and subframes that are given over to another purpose, such as Multicast-Broadcast Single Frequency Network (MBSFN) transmissions. The number of eCCEs that fit into one PRB pair is given by Table 1, below. Thus, for example, in a normal subframe with a normal CP length, localized transmission using aggregation levels of 1, 2, or 4 uses only a single PRB pair, while localized transmission using an aggregation level of 8 requires the use of two PRB pairs.

     In case the aggregation level of the ePDCCH is too large, a second PRB pair is used as well, and so on, using more PRB pairs, until all eCCEs belonging to the ePDCCH have been mapped.  FIG. 7B  illustrates an example of localized transmission. In this example, the same four parts of the ePDCCH are mapped to a single PRB pair. 
     As described above, certain downlink resources are made available for sending PDCCH and ePDCCH messages to the UE. However, a given UE is not targeted to receive control channel messages in every subframe. Further, the UE does not know in advance precisely where a control channel message will be located among the resources made available for the control channel messages. Thus, the UE must search for a control message that may not exist, in each of several possible locations for the message. The concept of a “search space” is used to define a range of possible locations for control messages, to keep the required amount of searching to a reasonable level.

     As is also the case for PDCCH, the ePDCCH is transmitted over radio resources shared by multiple UEs. The enhanced CCE (eCCE) is introduced as the equivalent of the CCE for PDCCH. Like a CCE, an eCCE also has a fixed number of resource elements. However, the number of resource elements actually available for ePDCCH mapping is generally fewer than the fixed number, because many resource elements are occupied by other signals such as Cell-specific Reference Signals (CRS) and Channel State Information-Reference Signal (CSI-RS). Code-chain rate matching is applied whenever a resource element belonging to an eCCE contains other colliding signals such as the CRS, CSI-RS, legacy control region or in case of Time Division Duplexing (TDD), the Guard Period (GP) and Uplink Pilot Time Slot (UpPTS). 
     Consider the example in  FIG. 8 , where item 40 illustrates the PDCCH mapping. The PDCCH always avoids the CRS, so that a CCE always contains T avial =36 available resource elements. In item 42, on the other hand, it is shown how an eCCE contains 36 resource elements nominally, but the number of available resource elements is reduced in the event that there are colliding signals. Hence, T avail ≦36 resource elements for ePDCCH. Since the colliding signals are subframe dependent, the value of T avail  becomes subframe dependent as well, and could even be different for different eCCEs, if the collisions impact on the eCCEs unevenly. It is noted that when the number of eCCEs per PRB pair is two (see Table 1), the nominal number of resource elements per eCCE is not 36, but instead is either 72 (for normal CP length) or 64 (for extended CP length).

     In distributed transmission, an ePDCCH can be mapped to resource elements in up to D PRB pairs, where D=2, 4, or 8 (the value of D=16 is also being considered in 3GPP). In this way, frequency diversity can be achieved for the ePDCCH message. See  FIG. 7A  for a schematic example in which a downlink subframe shows four parts belonging to an ePDCCH which is mapped to multiple of the enhanced control regions known as PRB pairs, to achieve distributed transmission and frequency diversity or sub-band precoding. 
     As of September 2012, the 3GPP has not reached agreement as to how four or eight eREGs respectively should be grouped into the eCCEs. It is also an open question as to how the encoded and modulated symbols of an ePDCCH message are mapped to the resource elements within the resources reserved by its associated eREGs. Further, the number of blind decodes per aggregation level for ePDCCH has not yet been decided in the 3GPP standardization work. Likewise, how randomization of the search space for localized and distributed mappings is generated has not yet been decided, although it is clear that overlap between ePDCCH candidates of different aggregation levels will occur also for the ePDCCH, as is the case for the PDCCH. 
     Time-Division Duplex (TDD) operation in LTE systems presents additional challenges with respect to PDCCH and ePDCCH to PUCCH mapping. These challenges to PUCCH HARQ-ACK resource determination arise from the asymmetry between uplink and downlink. When there are more downlink subframes than uplink subframes, the one to one mapping used in Frequency-Division Duplex (FDD) mode cannot be reused, since PUCCH resources selected according to this approach will collide with each other across different downlink subframes. On the other hand, overall HARQ-ACK resource utilization should be considered, since the resources for PUSCH transmission will be reduced if excessive uplink resources are reserved for PUCCH HARQ-ACK transmission. The TDD PUCCH resource for HARQ-ACK transmission in response to legacy PDCCH has been specified in the technical standardization document 3GPP TS 36.213, “Physical Layer Procedures,” v10.6.0. 
       FIG. 9  provides an illustration of the allocation of PUCCH resources for PDCCH, in TDD mode. The illustrated example is for four downlink subframes (SF 0 , SF 1 , SF 2 , and SF 3 ) and one uplink subframe (SF 4 ). Therein the resource determination for HARQ-ACK multiplexing and HARQ-ACK bundling are similar and can be derived as specified in 3GPP TS 36.213 v10.6.0, “Physical Layer Procedures”. It can be seen that the PUCCH HARQ-ACK resources will be stacked firstly for the lowest eCCE index of the DCI that fall within the first one-third CCEs of the control region, across multiple subframes (from SF  0  to SF  3 ) (marked with diagonal shading). These PUCCH HARQ-ACK resources are followed by the DCIs belonging to the second one-third CCEs of the control region (shaded). Finally are the last one-third CCEs (marked with cross-hatching). The design philosophy is that when system load is low, the control region could be automatically reduced by the dynamic signaling of PCFICH, hence the PUCCH HARQ-ACK resource could be compressed to a continuous region. 
     TDD PUCCH resource determination for ePDCCH has not been resolved in 3GPP RANI yet, i.e., no concrete solution is provided. However, a separate design different from FDD is needed, just as for PDCCH. Due to the fundamental differences in resource structures, the current design for PDCCH cannot be reused for ePDCCH. For example, PDCCH is a common control region (first one to four OFDM symbols) for all UEs while ePDCCH is multiplexed in frequency with PDSCH in a UE-specific manner. Accordingly, techniques for TDD PUCCH HARQ resource allocation for the Enhanced Physical Downlink Control Channel (ePDCCH) in radio communication systems are needed. 
     SUMMARY 
     According to several embodiments of the techniques disclosed herein, solutions are provided for PUCCH resource determination for HARQ-ACK transmission in response to ePDCCH-scheduled PDSCH or ePDCCH-indicated SPS release in a TDD radio communication system. Several different categories of embodiments are detailed below, each of which may have different combinations of PUCCH blocking probability, PUCCH resource utilization efficiency, eNB scheduler complexity and implementation complexity. 
     One example embodiment of the presently disclosed techniques is a processing method, suitable for implementation by a wireless device, for determining the resources for transmitting hybrid automatic-repeat-request (HARQ) feedback in a wireless communication network configured for time-division duplexing (TDD) operation. The example method begins with receiving downlink control information (DCI) via an Enhanced Physical Downlink Control Channel (ePDCCH) in a downlink subframe. The received ePDCCH schedules a downlink shared channel transmission to the wireless device or indicates a release of semi-persistent scheduling (SPS) to the wireless device. The method continues with determining a resource index for a Physical Uplink Control Channel (PUCCH) resource based on the lowest enhanced Control Channel Element (eCCE) index of the received DCI, a device-specific offset value previously signaled to the wireless device via Radio Resource Control (RRC) signaling, and an index i. The index i identifies the downlink subframe in a pre-determined set of one or more downlink subframes associated with an uplink subframe. The determining of the PUCCH resource is performed according to a formula that results in a sequential allocation of PUCCH resources in the uplink subframe with respect to the downlink subframes associated with the uplink subframe, for each of a plurality of sets of ePDCCH resources. The method continues with the transmitting of HARQ feedback in the uplink subframe, using a PUCCH resource that corresponds to the resource indek. 
     In some embodiments, determining the resource index for the PUCCH resource comprises determining the resource index based on the sum of (i) the lowest enhanced eCCE of the received DCI, (ii) the device-specific offset value previously signaled to the wireless device via RRC signaling, and (iii) the product of the index i and the number of eCCEs in a set of ePDCCH resources that includes those ePDCCH resources used by the received ePDCCH. In some of these embodiments, the set of ePDCCH resources is set q of a plurality of sets of ePDCCH resources, wherein the uplink subframe is subframe n and the downlink subframe is subframe n−k i , where k i  is the i-th element in the pre-determined set of downlink subframes associated with subframe n, the pre-determined set comprising M elements indexed according to k 0 , k 1 , . . . , k M-1 , and determining the resource index comprises calculating: n PUCCH,i   (1) =i·N q   eccE +n eCCE,i +N UE-PUCCH   (q) , where n eCCE,i  is the lowest eCCE index of the received DCI and N q   eCCE  is the number of eCCEs in ePDCCH set q. The resource index in these embodiments is derived from n PUCCH,i   (1) .

Following equation (3) above, the PUCCH HARQ-ACK resource will be stacked across subframes after each other per set q as shown in  FIG. 14 . Thus, the PUCCH ACK/NAK resources according to this embodiment are stacked for each ePDCCH set, one by one. Starting from the set with the lowest PUCCH ACK/NAK starting position, the PUCCH ACK/NAK resources are stacked across the subframes sequentially, i.e., DCI messages belonging to subframe  0  first followed by DCIs belonging to subframe  1 , etc. The set with second lowest PUCCH ACK/NAK starting position will be stacked beginning at the end of region for the first set, then the set with the third lowest PUCCH ACK/NAK starting position, etc. In  FIG. 14 , each of the different ePDCCH sets is indicated by diagonally-marked, shaded, and cross-hatched blocks. An advantage with this embodiment is that a single parameter N UE-PUCCH   (0)  is able to provide unique PUCCH resources for all of the different sets at the same time. Thus, there will be no resource collisions among different sets, as well as no resource collisions between subframes. 
     Embodiment 3 
     In this third embodiment and variants thereof, the PUCCH resources from the corresponding ePDCCH are stacked first within one subframe for all sets. This is quite distinct from embodiment 2, where the PUCCH resources are stacked per all subframes within a set. Thus, for PDSCH transmission indicated by the detection of corresponding ePDCCH or an ePDCCH indicating downlink SPS release within subframe n−k i , where k i  to a set of M elements k i ε{k 1 , k 2 , . . . , k M-1 } as defined in Table 10.1.3.1-1 in 3GPP TS 36.213, v10.6.0, the UE shall determine the PUCCH resource n PUCCH   (1)  for this third embodiment as follows: 
         n   PUCCH,i   (1)   =i·N   PUCCH   ePDCCH   +n   eCCE,i   +N   UE-PUCCH   (k) ,  (4)
 
     where n eCCE,i  belongs to ePDCCH set q of subframe n−k i , 0≦i≦M−1; M is the number of elements in the set defined in Table 10.1.3.1-1 of 3GPP TS 36.213, v. 10.6.0; and N PUCCH   ePDCCH  is the total number of PUCCH resources in all sets within one subframe. Following equation (4) above, the PUCCH HARQ-ACK resource in different subframes will not be overlapped as shown in the example of  FIG. 15 , again with diagonally-marked blocks indicating subframes belonging to a first set, shaded blocks indicating subframes belonging to a second set and cross-hatched blocks indicating subframes belonging to a third set. Thus, according to this embodiment, the PUCCH ACK/NAK resources are stacked for each subframe sequentially. Starting from subframe  0 , the PUCCH ACK/NAK resources are stacked separately for each set. Note that the size of the resource region within one subframe depends on the size of each ePDCCH set and the PUCCH starting position of each set. The PUCCH ACK/NAK resource for subframe  1  starts from the end of resource region for subframe  0  in the same manner, then subframe  2  is after subframe  1 , etc. N PUCCH   ePDCCH  can, for example, either be calculated by the UE based on all configured sets or signaled from the eNodeB. This solution also has low complexity. Compared to the first embodiment, there will be no resource collisions among different subframes but the resource utilization is relatively low, since the resources are reserved even when there is no user scheduled within a particular subframe.

     Among other things, the foregoing embodiments provide several solutions for PUCCH resource determination for HARQ-ACK transmission in response to ePDCCH-scheduled PDSCH or ePDCCH-indicated SPS release in a TDD system. These embodiments offer different alternatives with tradeoffs among, for example, PUCCH blocking probability, PUCCH resource utilization efficiency, eNB scheduler complexity and implementation complexity. 
     From the foregoing discussion of various exemplary embodiments, it will be appreciated that these and other embodiments will, when implemented, have impacts on various nodes in a radio communication system. For example, the various PUCCH resource determination schemes for HARQ-ACK transmission in response to ePDCCH-scheduled PDSCH or ePDCCH-indicated SPS release in a TDD system described above may need to be implemented at both a network side node (e.g., eNB) and at the user equipment. 
       FIG. 18  illustrates a non-limiting example embodiment of a processing method  1800 , which corresponds to the above-described processing for the wireless device  12 , for at least embodiment 1. The method  1800  is directed to a technique for determining the resources for transmitting hybrid automatic-repeat-request (HARQ) feedback in a wireless communication network configured for time-division duplexing (TDD) operation. The method begins, as shown at block  1810 , with receiving downlink control information (DCI) via an Enhanced Physical Downlink Control Channel (ePDCCH) in a downlink subframe. The received ePDCCH schedules a downlink shared channel transmission to the wireless device or indicates a release of semi-persistent scheduling (SPS) to the wireless device. 
     As shown at block  1820 , the method continues with determining a resource index for a Physical Uplink Control Channel (PUCCH) resource based on the lowest enhanced Control Channel Element (eCCE) index of the received DCI, a device-specific offset value previously signaled to the wireless device via Radio Resource Control (RRC) signaling, and an index i. The index i identifies the downlink subframe in a pre-determined set of one or more downlink subframes associated with an uplink subframe. The determining of the PUCCH resource is performed according to a formula that results in a sequential allocation of PUCCH resources in the uplink subframe with respect to the downlink subframes associated with the uplink subframe, for each of a plurality of sets of ePDCCH resources. As shown at block  1830 , the method continues with the transmitting of HARQ feedback in the uplink subframe, using a PUCCH resource that corresponds to the resource index. 
     In some embodiments, such as those described above under the heading “Embodiment 1,” determining the resource index for the PUCCH resource comprises determining the resource index based on the sum of (i) the lowest enhanced eCCE of the received DCI, (ii) the device-specific offset value previously signaled to the wireless device via RRC signaling, and (iii) the product of the index i and the number of eCCEs in a set of ePDCCH resources that includes those ePDCCH resources used by the received ePDCCH. In some of these embodiments, determining the resource index comprises calculating the resource index according to equation (2), as set forth above. 
     As noted earlier, the operations carried out by a wireless device  12  in determining the PUCCH resource and transmitting HARQ feedback in that resource are complemented by corresponding operations in a network node  10 , e.g., an LTE eNB, in determining the PUCCH resource used by the wireless device  12  and receiving the HARQ feedback in that resource.  FIG. 19  thus illustrates a non-limiting example embodiment of a processing method  1900 , which corresponds to this processing for a network node  10 , for at least embodiment 1. Method  1900  is thus generally directed to a technique for determining the resources for receiving hybrid automatic-repeat-request (HARQ) feedback in a wireless communication network configured for time-division duplexing (TDD) operation. The method begins, as shown at block  1910 , with transmitting downlink control information (DCI) to a wireless device, via an Enhanced Physical Downlink Control Channel (ePDCCH) in a downlink subframe. The transmitted ePDCCH schedules a downlink shared channel transmission to the wireless device or indicates a release of semi-persistent scheduling (SPS) to the wireless device. 
     As shown at block  1920 , the method continues with determining a resource index for a Physical Uplink Control Channel (PUCCH) resource based on the lowest enhanced Control Channel Element (eCCE) index of the transmitted DCI, a device-specific offset value previously signaled to the wireless device via Radio Resource Control (RRC) signaling, and an index i. The index i identifies the downlink subframe in a pre-determined set of one or more downlink subframes associated with an uplink subframe. The determining of the PUCCH resource is performed according to a formula that results in a sequential allocation of PUCCH resources in the uplink subframe with respect to the downlink subframes associated with the uplink subframe, for each of a plurality of sets of ePDCCH resources. As shown at block  1910 , the method continues with the receiving of HARQ feedback in the uplink subframe, using a PUCCH resource that corresponds to the resource index. 
     In some embodiments, such as those described above under the heading “Embodiment 1,” determining the resource index for the PUCCH resource comprises determining the resource index based on the sum of (i) the lowest enhanced eCCE of the transmitted DCI, (ii) the device-specific offset value previously signaled to the wireless device via RRC signaling, and (iii) the product of the index i and the number of eCCEs in a set of ePDCCH resources that includes those ePDCCH resources used by the transmitted ePDCCH. In some of these embodiments, determining the resource index comprises calculating the resource index according to equation (2), as set forth above. 
     With the above examples in mind, it should be clear that the teachings herein provide several solutions for PUCCH resource determination for HARQ-ACK transmission in response to ePDCCH-scheduled PDSCH or ePDCCH-indicated SPS release in a TDD system. The different alternatives provide different tradeoffs among PUCCH blocking probability, PUCCH resource utilization efficiency, eNB scheduler complexity and implementation complexity.

prior_art.abstract: Technology for transmitting a distributed control channel element (CCE) for an enhanced physical downlink control channel (ePDCCH) and a localized CCE in a physical resource block (PRB) pair from a node and technology for physical downlink shared channel (PDSCH) physical resource block (PRB) allocation with at least one enhanced physical downlink control channel (ePDCCH) at a wireless device is disclosed. One method can include a node precoding at least one distributed CCE and at least one localized CCE for the PRB pair. The node can transmit the at least one distributed CCE for transmit diversity using at least two user equipment-specific reference signal (UERS) ports and transmitting the at least one localized CCE in the PRB pair. The at least two UERS ports can be used to transmit two CCEs.
