     Various embodiments of methods, apparatus, and computer-readable storage media for rendering a map according to hybrid map data are described. Several embodiments of map rendering are described that may be suitable for rendering hybrid map data, which may contain raster graphics data and vector graphics data. In some embodiments, hybrid map data may be obtained as map tiles. Hybrid map data may be rendered to display a two-dimensional or three-dimensional map view of a map. 
     A map service, or server, may generate hybrid map data. Within the hybrid map data may be one or more features. Features of maps may be various objects in a map, such as coast lines, park boundaries, roads, or labels. In some embodiments, features may overlap one another. Features may also border one another, covering distinct areas within hybrid map data. Generating hybrid map data may, in some embodiments, determine for each feature within the hybrid map data whether the feature is to be described according to vector graphics. To make this determination, at least some embodiments may calculate the number of geometric primitives necessary to render the feature according to vector graphics. Generally, geographic primitives used in vector graphics include, but are not limited to, lines, curves, vertices, polygons, or shapes. Then, determining whether number of geographic primitives necessary to render a layer exceeds a complexity threshold value may indicate whether the feature is too complex to be generated using vector graphics. In some embodiments equaling or exceeding the complexity threshold value identifies the feature as too complex for vector graphics data. A complexity threshold value may be determined according to the rendering capability or communication capability of a client device. Features of the hybrid map data are then generated. Features not determined to be described using vector graphics may be described using raster graphics. Features determined to be described using vector graphics may be described using vector graphics. Generated hybrid map data may be sent to a client device for rendering. 
     Some embodiments may implement rendering a map according to hybrid map data within a map service operating environment. Embodiments of a map service may be implemented in any application or service that sends map data to a client device. Example categories of applications in which embodiments may be implemented are navigation applications, such as those based upon the Global Positioning System (GPS) that display routes or directions for different types of vehicles or pedestrians, weather applications, or other applications displaying information in geographic space. Embodiments of a map service may be implemented as a module in an application that may be called by other applications or modules. For example, some applications may utilize the map service and provide further processing on the hybrid map data sent by the service before sending the hybrid map data to a client device. 
     A client device, in some embodiments, may obtain hybrid map data that contains raster graphics data and vector graphics data. A client device may render a map view based upon the hybrid map data. For hybrid map data containing vector graphics data, a client device may render the data according to vector graphics. For hybrid map data containing raster graphics data, a client device may render data according to raster graphics. Embodiments may combine the rendered raster graphics data and the rendered vector graphics data to create a map view. Embodiments may then display the rendered map view on a display device. In some embodiments a client device may request hybrid map data from a map service or server. Other embodiments may obtain the hybrid map data automatically, without requesting it from a map service. A client device may also obtain hybrid map data from local storage. Hybrid map data may also be partially obtained from a map service and partially obtained from another source, such as another module or application on the client device or another from another device, such as another client device. 
     In at least some embodiments, a client device may obtain input modifying a displayed map view. The modification may be a modification to the zoom level of a displayed map view. In response to obtaining the input, the client device may render the vector graphics data according to the modified zoom level and scale the raster graphics data according to the modified zoom level. Embodiments may then combine the rendered vector graphics data with the scale raster graphics data to create a modified map view. In some embodiments, a client device may request updated raster graphics data from a server or map service. Upon receiving the updated graphics data, embodiments may combine the rendered vector graphics data with the updated raster graphics data to create an updated map view. Some embodiments may display the updated map view. 
     Various embodiments of the hybrid map data may contain raster graphics data that describes a background layer and vector graphics data describing one or more objects overlaying the background layer. Some embodiments of hybrid map data may contain other raster graphics data used to render a fill portion of at least one of the one or more objects described by the vector graphics data. 
     Embodiments of a client device may be implemented in an application on computing or electronic devices, such as portable multifunction devices, including but not limited to, an iPod®, iPhone®, or iPad® devices from Apple Inc. of Cupertino, California. Some example embodiments may implement a client device as a module within an application, such as a navigation system that provides routing information and direction information to a user, or a map application which displays multiple map views for a user. Embodiments may also implement the client device as a module that may be called by other applications or modules, such as a weather application. A client device may communicate with a map service as part of a map service operating environment. 
     Map Service Operating Environment 
     Various embodiments may operate within a map service operating environment.  FIG. 1  illustrates a map service operating environment, according to some embodiments. A map service  130  may provide map services for one or more client devices  102   a - 102   c  in communication with the map service  130  through various communication methods and protocols. A map service  130  generally may provide map information and other map-related data, such as two-dimensional map image data (e.g., aerial view of roads utilizing satellite imagery), three-dimensional map image data (e.g., traversable map with three-dimensional features, such as buildings), route and direction calculation (e.g., ferry route calculations or directions between two points for a pedestrian), real-time navigation data (e.g., turn-by-turn visual navigation data in two or three dimensions), location data (e.g., where is the client device currently located), and other geographic data (e.g., wireless network coverage, weather, traffic information, or nearby points-of-interest). In various embodiments, the map service data may include localized labels for different countries or regions; localized labels may be utilized to present map labels (e.g., street names, city names, points of interest) in different languages on client devices. Client devices  102   a - 102   c  may utilize these map services by obtaining map service data. Client devices  102   a - 102   c  may implement various techniques to process map service data. Client devices  102   a - 102   c  may then provide map services to various entities, including, but not limited to, users, internal software or hardware modules, and/or other systems or devices external to the client devices  102   a - 102   c.    
     In some embodiments, a map service may be implemented by one or more nodes in a distributed computing system. Each node may be assigned one or more services or components of a map service. Some nodes may be assigned the same map service or component of a map service. A load balancing node may distribute access or requests to other nodes within a map service. In some embodiments a map service may be implemented as a single system, such as a single server. Different modules or hardware devices within a server may implement one or more of the various services provided by a map service. 
     A map service may provide map services by generating map service data in various formats. In some embodiments, one format of map service data may be map image data. Map image data may provide image data to a client device so that the client device may process the image data (e.g., rendering and/or displaying the image data as a two-dimensional or three-dimensional map). Map image data, whether in two or three dimensions, may specify one or more map tiles. A map tile may be a portion of a larger map image. Assembling together the map tiles of a map may produce the original map. Tiles may be generated from map image data, routing or navigation data, or any other map service data. In some embodiments map tiles may be raster-based map tiles, with tile sizes ranging from any size both larger and smaller than a commonly-used 256 pixel by 256 pixel tile. Raster-based map tiles may be encoded in any number of standard digital image representations including, but not limited to, Bitmap (.bmp), Graphics Interchange Format (.gif), Joint Photographic Experts Group (.jpg, .jpeg, etc.), Portable Networks Graphic (.png), or Tagged Image File Format (.tiff). In some embodiments, map tiles may be vector-based map tiles, encoded using vector graphics, including, but not limited to, Scalable Vector Graphics (.svg) or a Drawing File (.drw). Embodiments may also include tiles with a combination of vector and raster data. Metadata or other information pertaining to the map tile may also be included within or along with a map tile, providing further map service data to a client device. In various embodiments, a map tile may be encoded for transport utilizing various standards and/or protocols, some of which are described in examples below. 
     In various embodiments, map tiles may be constructed from image data of different resolutions depending on zoom level. For instance, for low zoom level (e.g., world or globe view), the resolution of map or image data need not be as high relative to the resolution at a high zoom level (e.g., city or street level). For example, when in a globe view, there may be no need to render street level artifacts as such objects would be so small as to be negligible in many cases. 
     A map service may perform various techniques to analyze a map tile before encoding the tile for transport. This analysis may optimize map service performance for both client devices and a map service. In some embodiments map tiles may be analyzed for complexity, according to vector-based graphic techniques, and constructed utilizing complex and non-complex layers. Map tiles may also be analyzed for common image data or patterns that may be rendered as image textures and constructed by relying on image masks. In some embodiments, raster-based image data in a map tile may contain certain mask values, which are associate with one or more textures. Embodiments may also analyze map tiles for specified features that may be associated with certain map styles that contain style identifiers.

     Generating Hybrid Map Data 
     Embodiments of rendering a map according to hybrid map data may operate within a map service operating environment, such as described above with regard to  FIG. 1 . A map service, as stated previously may generally may provide map information and other map-related data, such as two-dimensional map image data (e.g., aerial view of roads utilizing satellite imagery), three-dimensional map image data (e.g., traversable map with three-dimensional features, such as buildings), route and direction calculation (e.g., ferry route calculations or directions between two points for a pedestrian), real-time navigation data (e.g., turn-by-turn visual navigation data in two or three dimensions), location data (e.g., where is the client device currently located), and other geographic data (e.g., wireless network coverage, weather, traffic information, or nearby points-of-interest). In various embodiments a map service, such as map service  130  described above with regard to  FIG. 1 , may provide hybrid map data to a client device. 
     According to various embodiments,  FIG. 2  outlines a method for generating hybrid map data which may be implemented on a map service or server, such as map service  130  described in  FIG. 1 . Hybrid map data contains raster graphics data and vector graphics data. Hybrid map data may be used to describe maps that contain features. Each feature may be distinct from any other feature in the map data. Features, as stated previously, may be an object of a map, such as a coastline or a park outline. Features may also be map features, such as interstates, railroads, or ferry lines. Features may be geographically displayed data, such as weather fronts, heat maps, or home sale prices, or other maps, such as airplane routes. In short, features may be any graphical image or annotation displayed on a map view of a map. A feature may be two-dimensional or three-dimensional image data. Embodiments may for each feature of the map determine whether the area is to be generated according to vector graphics  210 . 
     To determine whether a feature of a map is to be described using vector graphics, various methods may be user. In one such method, embodiments may calculate the number geometric primitives necessary to render the feature according to vector graphics. A feature of hybrid map data as stored on a map service may be composed of raster graphics data. To determine the number of necessary geometric primitives for the area based on the raster data, embodiments may employ various processes on various hardware and software configurations known to persons having ordinary skill in the art that perform vectorization, and thus converting raster data into vector data. For example, embodiments may implement vectorization relying on, but not limited to, thresholding, thinning, contour tracing, and skeletonization algorithms to extract geometric primitives. These geometric primitives may include lines, curves, vertices, polygons, such as triangles, or other shapes. After vectorization, by assembling these geometric primitives an area may be represented according to vector graphics and thus the number of these geometric primitives may be determined. 
     Embodiments may also calculate the number geometric primitives for an feature of hybrid map data stored on a map service composed of vector graphics data. To calculate the number of geometric primitives necessary according to render the feature, some embodiments may parse the vector data and count the number of geometric primitives. Some embodiments may only count certain primitives, as some primitives may render faster than others. Embodiments may also only count certain primitives because not all vector primitives are supported in all vector data file formats. In some embodiments, vector vertices are counted to determine the number of geometric primitives necessary to render the feature according to vector graphics. 
     Various embodiments may determine whether the calculated number of geometric primitives exceeds a complexity threshold value to indicate whether the feature is too complex to generate using vector graphics. This complexity threshold value may be a singular value applicable to all map features in a particular set of map data, given map, or for all maps. Some embodiments may store multiple complexity threshold values and select a value based upon information about the map or client device. Embodiments may receive a request for map data from a client device. Within the request may be client capability indications, such as rendering capability or communication capability indications, so that when communicating with a client device, information identifying the hardware components of a client device may be determined by a map service. For example, embodiments of a complexity threshold value may store multiple values in a table indexed to client device type. Different values in the table may correspond to the different rendering capabilities of different devices. In some embodiments, communication capability, such as the data transfer bandwidth of the map service operating environment, such as map service operating environment  100  or the client device  102  in  FIG. 1 , may determine the complexity threshold value. Embodiments may also have other modules or applications internal or external to the map service that supply or select the complexity threshold value. Some embodiments may implement various combinations of information about rendering capability and data transfer bandwidth to select a complexity threshold value. 
     The determination of whether the calculated number of geometric primitives exceeds a complexity threshold value may be implemented by performing a relational operation, including but not limited to, whether the complexity threshold value is less than, less than or equals to, greater than, or greater than or equals to the determined number of geometric primitives. Some embodiments may implement the determination through hardware or software implementations. The result of the determination indicates whether the area is too complex to generate using vector graphics. 
     If after determining that the area of the map is not to be described according to vector graphics  210 , a map service may generate a description of the map feature using raster graphics  212 . Raster graphics, as described above, encode image values of pixels in the image. Common raster graphics formats that a map service may implement are bitmaps, JPEG, PNG, or GIF. If after determining that the feature of the map is to be described according to vector graphics  210 , a map service may generate the map area using vector graphics  214 . Vector graphics, as described above, use descriptive functions to encode an image. A map service may implement various vector graphics formats for areas, such as SVG or DRW formats. However, the above raster and vector graphic formats are examples only and not intended to be limiting. If each map feature of the hybrid map data has been generated  220 , then the hybrid map data is generated. 
     Various embodiments send the hybrid map data to a client device for rendering  230 . Some embodiments may utilize the communication channels of a map service operating environment, such as described in  FIG. 1 . For example, hybrid map data may be sent over a wide area network, such as the Internet  100  in  FIG. 1 , to client devices, such as client devices  102  through wireless and wired access points. Hybrid map data may be sent in multiple sizes or file formats and may represent two-dimensional and three-dimensional map data. Some embodiments may send maps as map tiles. In some embodiments the format of hybrid map data may be map tiles. Map tiles are generally portions of a map divided into tiles which are assembled together to display a map. A map tile is commonly, but not limited to, 256×256 pixels display size. Map tiles may include two or more areas. Embodiments may send map tiles that contain vector graphics data, raster graphics data, or a combination of both to a client device as hybrid map data. 
     Rendering Hybrid Map Data 
     A client device, such as client device  102  in  FIG. 1 , may obtain from a server, such as a map service  130 , hybrid map data and render the hybrid map data for display. According to various embodiments  FIG. 3  outlines a method for rendering hybrid map data according to some embodiments. A client device may obtain from a server hybrid map data containing raster graphics data and vector graphics data. In some embodiments, a client device may request hybrid map data using the communication channels of a map service operating environment, such as discussed above with regard to  FIG. 1 . Some embodiments may obtain hybrid map data stored on the client device, while some embodiments obtain hybrid map data from another client device through peer-to-peer communications, such as the peer-to-peer communications discussed above with regard to  FIG. 1 . Hybrid map data, as discussed above, may be represented in various data structures and graphic formats. Hybrid map data may describe two-dimensional or three-dimensional map data. Some hybrid map data may be obtained as map tiles. 
     Once the hybrid map data is obtained, as indicated at  310 , a client device may render a map view based upon the obtained hybrid map data for display on a display device, such as a touch-sensitive display  1012  described with regard to  FIG. 9 . A client device may render the raster data using raster graphics techniques  320 . Rendering according to raster graphics is performed according to techniques well known to those of ordinary skill in the art. As raster image formats may be represented as bitmaps, less processing is necessary to prepare a raster image. For example, some embodiments may send areas encoded utilizing raster graphics directly to a frame buffer, or other device, that outputs the layer to a display without any further processing. Embodiments may also store the raster area on the client device, or combine the raster area with vector areas that have been rasterized according to vector graphics. It will be apparent to those of ordinary skill in the art that many different software and hardware modules, applications, or devices may be utilized to render data of hybrid map data composed of raster graphics data. 
     Client device may then render the vector data using vector graphics techniques  330 . Vector data may be encoded using well known vector image formats, such as Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG). A client device may implement various hardware and software techniques to render the vector data, well known to persons of ordinary skill in the art, including, but not limited to, an implementation of Open Graphics Library (OpenGL) which allows for a hardware independent implementation of rendering applications. Various devices, such as a Graphics Processing Unit (GPU), may be optimized by embodiments to render vector data. Common vectorization techniques, such as those discussed above, may be employed by a client device to render vector data of the hybrid data using vector graphics  330 . 
     Various embodiments may then combine the rendered raster graphics data with the rendered vector graphics data to create the map view  340 . In some embodiments the raster graphics data may be a background layer, and vector graphics may describe one or more objects overlaying the background layer. For example, a device may receive hybrid map data where the raster data describes an urban area, with houses, buildings, and other map objects. The vector graphics data may over lay roads, railroads, and other transportation paths as vector objects on top of the background layer. Some embodiments may obtain additional raster graphics data to render a fill portion of vector objects. For example, hybrid map data may contain a vector object described by vector graphics data that gives the outline of a park. The additional raster graphics data in the hybrid map data may contain a fill texture for the park. 
     Various embodiments may then display the rendered map view  350  on a display device, such as a touch-sensitive display  1012  described with regard to  FIG. 9 . The displayed map view may be a two-dimensional or three-dimensional map view of a map. It may comprise various features, such as roads, parks, lakes, paths, in various modes, such as navigation mode, night mode, pedestrian mode, current weather mode, or terrain mode. Some embodiments may obtain input modifying the displayed map view. In some embodiments this modification includes a display instruction. A display instruction may change a zoom level. For example, a display instruction may zoom the map from a high aerial view to a close view. A display instruction may also comprise a change in the map view orientation. For example, instead of the map view being displayed as oriented facing north, a display instruction may modify the map view orientation to face east. Other various display instructions in a map view modification are envisioned, such as select a different map view mode, or modifying map view display preferences. 
     Input modifying the displayed map view may be obtained through various input devices, such as touch (e.g. touch-sensitive display  1012  in  FIG. 9 ), or any of the other myriad input devices described with regard to  FIGS. 7 through 10 .  FIG. 4  illustrates a flowchart of a method of rendering hybrid map data in response to a modification of the map display according to some embodiments. Some embodiments may obtain input modifying a zoom level of the displayed map view  362 . This input may be by one of the various input devices described above. Embodiments may then, in response to the input, render a modified map view based upon the obtained hybrid map data. To render a modified map view, embodiments may render the vector graphics data  364  according to the modified zoom level. For example, to increase a zoom for a vector line, line simplification techniques may be employed. Embodiments may scale the raster graphics data  366  according to the modified zoom level. For example, if the zoom level is increased, the raster data will be resized larger. Embodiments may then combine the rendered vector graphics data and the scaled raster graphics data  368 . Embodiments may then display the modified map view  370  on a display device, such as touch-sensitive display device  1012  in  FIG. 9 . 
     Some embodiments may request from server, such as map service  130  in  FIG. 1 , updated raster graphics data  372  that corresponds to the modified zoom level. For example, if the zoom level is increased, a request may be made for higher resolution raster graphics data. In response to receiving the updated raster graphics data, embodiments may combine the render vector graphics data, indicated at  364 , with the updated raster graphics data  374  to create an updated map view. Some embodiments may then display the updated map view  376  on a display device, such as touch-sensitive display device  1012  in  FIG. 9 . 
     Example Embodiments 
     Various embodiments may implement a method for generating hybrid data such as described in  FIG. 2 , in a module.  FIG. 5  illustrates one such embodiment. A map service module  400  may be implemented on a computer or electronic device, such as a system described below with regard to  FIG. 11 . A map service module  400  may be implemented on one or more nodes of a distributed map service system. The map service module  400  may also be one of many modules in an application. Embodiments may implement communications between these other modules  404  and the map service module  400 , such as those communication channels described with respect to  FIG. 1 . 
     A hybrid map data  410  may be generated by the map service  400  or sent to the map service  400  by another module/application/system  404 , or client device  402 . A client device, such as client device  102  described above with respect to  FIG. 1 , may request hybrid map data  410 . Hybrid map data may describe a map with features. Hybrid map data  410  may be composed of vector graphics data and raster graphics data. Hybrid map data  410  may also be composed of map tiles. Embodiments may select a hybrid map data feature  412  to generate a representation. The map service module  400  may then calculate the number of vector vertices necessary to render the feature according to vector graphics  414 , according to one of the various methods discussed above with regard to  FIG. 2 . Vector vertices are commonly used to construct other geometric primitives used by vector graphics. For example, OpenGL interprets a list of vertices, a vertex stream, into geometric primitives as defined by a programmer. 
     A map service module  400  may then compare the determined number of vertices  416  to the complexity threshold value  417 . The complexity threshold value  417  may be determined according to information obtained from a client device  402 . Information about a client device may be sent to a module  400 , such as in a request for a hybrid map data  410 . Included in this information, but not limited to, may be hardware or software information, such as operating system name/version, device type (mobile phone, PDA, or desktop computer), Central Processing Unit (CPU) or Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) capabilities, or client device driver information. Communication capabilities between the map service module  400  and the client device  402  may also be indicated by the bandwidth of transferring data between the module  400  and the client device  402 . The module may implement hardware or software processes to select a complexity threshold value  417  among the possible information received about the client device itself or communication capabilities between the module and the client device. In various embodiments, if the calculated number is greater than or equal to the complexity threshold value  418 , then the selected feature may be generated using raster graphics description  422 . Otherwise the feature may be generated using vector graphics description  420 . Formats and techniques for generating raster and vector graphics are discussed above with regard to  FIG. 2 .

The map service module  400  may then send then the hybrid map data to a client device  402  using one of the many communication channels discussed above with regard to  FIG. 1  for rendering at the client device.

     In some embodiments, event sorter  1070  also includes a hit view determination module  1072  and/or an active event recognizer determination module  1073 . 
     Hit view determination module  1072  provides software procedures for determining where a sub-event has taken place within one or more views, when touch sensitive display  1012  displays more than one view. Views are made up of controls and other elements that a user can see on the display. 
     Another aspect of the user interface associated with an application is a set of views, sometimes herein called application views or user interface windows, in which information is displayed and touch-based gestures occur. The application views (of a respective application) in which a touch is detected may correspond to programmatic levels within a programmatic or view hierarchy of the application. For example, the lowest level view in which a touch is detected may be called the hit view, and the set of events that are recognized as proper inputs may be determined based, at least in part, on the hit view of the initial touch that begins a touch-based gesture. 
     Hit view determination module  1072  receives information related to sub-events of a touch-based gesture. When an application has multiple views organized in a hierarchy, hit view determination module  1072  identifies a hit view as the lowest view in the hierarchy which should handle the sub-event. In most circumstances, the hit view is the lowest level view in which an initiating sub-event occurs (i.e., the first sub-event in the sequence of sub-events that form an event or potential event). Once the hit view is identified by the hit view determination module, the hit view typically receives all sub-events related to the same touch or input source for which it was identified as the hit view. 
     Active event recognizer determination module  1073  determines which view or views within a view hierarchy should receive a particular sequence of sub-events. In some embodiments, active event recognizer determination module  1073  determines that only the hit view should receive a particular sequence of sub-events. In other embodiments, active event recognizer determination module  1073  determines that all views that include the physical location of a sub-event are actively involved views, and therefore determines that all actively involved views should receive a particular sequence of sub-events. In other embodiments, even if touch sub-events were entirely confined to the area associated with one particular view, views higher in the hierarchy would still remain as actively involved views.

     A respective event recognizer  1080  receives event information (e.g., event data  1079 ) from event sorter  1070 , and identifies an event from the event information.      Event receiver  1082  receives event information from event sorter  1070 . The event information includes information about a sub-event, for example, a touch or a touch movement. Depending on the sub-event, the event information also includes additional information, such as location of the sub-event. When the sub-event concerns motion of a touch the event information may also include speed and direction of the sub-event. In some embodiments, events include rotation of the device from one orientation to another (e.g., from a portrait orientation to a landscape orientation, or vice versa), and the event information includes corresponding information about the current orientation (also called device attitude) of the device. 
     Event comparator  1084  compares the event information to predefined event or sub-event definitions and, based on the comparison, determines an event or sub-event, or determines or updates the state of an event or sub-event. In some embodiments, event comparator  1084  includes event definitions  1086 . Event definitions  1086  contain definitions of events (e.g., predefined sequences of sub-events), for example, event 1 ( 1087 - 1 ), event 2 ( 1087 - 2 ), and others. In some embodiments, sub-events in an event  1087  include, for example, touch begin, touch end, touch movement, touch cancellation, and multiple touching. In one example, the definition for event 1 ( 1087 - 1 ) is a double tap on a displayed object. The double tap, for example, includes a first touch (touch begin) on the displayed object for a predetermined phase, a first lift-off (touch end) for a predetermined phase, a second touch (touch begin) on the displayed object for a predetermined phase, and a second lift-off (touch end) for a predetermined phase. In another example, the definition for event 2 ( 1087 - 2 ) is a dragging on a displayed object. The dragging, for example, includes a touch (or contact) on the displayed object for a predetermined phase, a movement of the touch across touch-sensitive display  1012 , and lift-off of the touch (touch end). In some embodiments, the event also includes information for one or more associated event handlers  1090 . 
     In some embodiments, event definition  1087  includes a definition of an event for a respective user-interface object. In some embodiments, event comparator  1084  performs a hit test to determine which user-interface object is associated with a sub-event. For example, in an application view in which three user-interface objects are displayed on touch-sensitive display  1012 , when a touch is detected on touch-sensitive display  1012 , event comparator  1084  performs a hit test to determine which of the three user-interface objects is associated with the touch (sub-event). If each displayed object is associated with a respective event handler  1090 , the event comparator uses the result of the hit test to determine which event handler  1090  should be activated. For example, event comparator  1084  selects an event handler associated with the sub-event and the object triggering the hit test. 
     In some embodiments, the definition for a respective event  1087  also includes delayed actions that delay delivery of the event information until after it has been determined whether the sequence of sub-events does or does not correspond to the event recognizer's event type. 
     When a respective event recognizer  1080  determines that the series of sub-events do not match any of the events in event definitions  1086 , the respective event recognizer  1080  enters an event impossible, event failed, or event ended state, after which it disregards subsequent sub-events of the touch-based gesture. In this situation, other event recognizers, if any, that remain active for the hit view continue to track and process sub-events of an ongoing touch-based gesture.

cases.title: Method for controlling a vehicle headlamp system
cases.abstract: A method for operating an electronically-controlled headlamp system of a motor vehicle capable of generating different light distributions, including a high-beam distribution and a low-beam distribution. The roadway region illuminated by the headlamps during the adjustment of the high-beam distribution comprises a high-beam region and a dimmed region, and the border between the high-beam region and the dimmed region is defined by at least one high-beam edge. An electronic headlamp controller is operable to displace or move the high-beam edge at a rate that is variable depending on a current driving scenario. The driving scenario may include a condition of a vehicle environment, a traffic scenario, a vehicle state, and an activity of vehicle driver. The transition duration between two different light intensities, the light-intensity adaptation, and the separation between a high-beam edge and an object (such as another vehicle), may also be varied depending on the driving scenario.

claims.text:
